clue.text: After homework, are to get ready

indicators.note: After places the word are behind the homework word in the answer

parts.note: prep is school slang for homework, short for preparation

explanation.surface: A pupil's instruction: once homework is done, it's time to get ready.
explanation.definitionFit: To prepare something is to make it fit for use, a synonym of making ready.

clue.text: Took part of Ham?

parts.note: reads like playing a role in a play called Ham, but a ham actor is one who exaggerates every line

explanation.walkthrough: The capital H dresses 'Ham' as a title (perhaps Hamlet cut short), but a ham is a bad actor who plays everything too big.
explanation.definitionFit: A ham actor exaggerates a performance, which is what doing too much on stage means.

clue.text: A fabric woven freely

parts.note: twill is a fabric woven with a diagonal ribbed pattern

explanation.surface: A loosely woven cloth described as hanging freely.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something whenever one likes means acting freely, without constraint.

clue.text: Going no distance by the river first for a medicinal plant

indicators.note: first says the river comes at the front of the answer, before the other pieces

parts.note: the Cam is the river that flows through Cambridge
O is the figure zero, meaning none
a mile is a measure of distance

explanation.surface: Someone who has stayed put beside the river seeks a herbal remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going' is a link here; 'no distance' splits into O (nought) and MILE.
explanation.definitionFit: Camomile is a daisy-like herb whose flowers are brewed as a soothing tea.

clue.text: Out once or twice

parts.note: a single cricket dismissal in which the bowler both delivers the ball and catches it, so it is one out achieved two ways

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a batsman is out this way when the bowler catches the ball off their own delivery: one dismissal, but credited to the bowler twice over.
explanation.definitionFit: This cricket dismissal is one wicket earned by two actions of the same player, bowling and catching.

clue.text: Doctor, I'm unwell, here's the spot

indicators.note: unwell suggests the letters are out of sorts and must be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A patient tells the doctor they feel ill and points to a blemish.
explanation.definitionFit: A microdot is a photograph shrunk to the size of a dot, used to hide documents.

clue.text: Mother with an afterthought names the disease

parts.note: mum is an informal word for mother
PS, postscript, is the afterthought added at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: A mother adds a note at the end of her letter naming an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: Mumps is a viral infection that swells the glands of the neck.

clue.text: Majority shareholder's partner?

parts.note: the lion's share is the largest portion, so the one taking it is a lion, whose mate is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a business colleague, but the 'lion's share' is the majority, so the shareholder is a lion and the partner its female mate.
explanation.definitionFit: The female of the big cat that takes the biggest portion is its natural mate.

clue.text: I treat first pair of hedge bushes

indicators.note: first puts the pair abbreviation ahead of the other words

parts.note: a vet treats sick animals, so to vet is to treat

explanation.surface: A gardener says they'll tend the first two hedges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first pair of' looks like a selection of the first two letters of 'hedge', but 'pair' gives the abbreviation PR and 'first' places it.
explanation.definitionFit: Privet is the evergreen shrub most commonly planted to form garden hedges.

clue.text: Remarkable but strange in Scotland having Frenchman coming before Scotsman

indicators.note: coming before says the Frenchman's letter sits ahead of the Scotsman in the answer

parts.note: unco is a Scots word for strange or unusual
M is the abbreviation for Monsieur, a Frenchman
mon is a stock dialect address for a Scotsman, as in 'hoots mon'

explanation.surface: Seems like a story of a Frenchman meeting a Scot in Scotland, described as odd.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unusual is out of the ordinary and so worth remarking on.

clue.text: Fairly willing to take risks?

parts.note: describes someone game for a gamble, while hinting at fair play

explanation.walkthrough: The word wanted means both fair-minded (a good loser) and ready to gamble, as in a sporting chance.
explanation.definitionFit: A sporting person plays fair and is ready to take a bet or a chance.

clue.text: Shellfish might mean the world to someone

definitions.meaning: a bivalve mollusc that can produce pearls

definitions.text: might mean the world to someone
definitions.meaning: from the saying that the world is your ..., meaning everything is open to you

explanation.definitionFit: It is an edible bivalve, and in Shakespeare's saying the whole world is one waiting to be opened.

clue.text: Couple allowed an ornamental chain

parts.note: a brace is a pair or couple, as of game birds
let means allowed

explanation.surface: A pair are permitted to wear a decorative chain.
explanation.definitionFit: A bracelet is a band or chain of jewellery worn round the wrist.

clue.text: Gradually pay off store I am converting

indicators.note: converting says these letters are changed into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper refitting a shop plans to clear the loan bit by bit.
explanation.definitionFit: To amortise a debt is to clear it in regular instalments over time.

clue.text: Partner is about to become known

indicators.note: about signals the preceding letters are turned around and rearranged

explanation.surface: A colleague is on the point of being revealed.
explanation.definitionFit: When a fact transpires it comes to light or emerges.

clue.text: England's patron gets ordered about before alternative example is put up

indicators.note: before places the shuffled letters ahead of the remaining pieces
ordered about says the letters of gets are shuffled

parts.note: or introduces an alternative

indicators.note: in a down clue, put up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: eg is the abbreviation for for example

explanation.surface: England's saint is bossed around ahead of some other illustration being erected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered about' makes STGE from GETS; 'is put up' turns EG into GE.
explanation.definitionFit: St George is the patron saint of England, famed for slaying a dragon.

clue.text: Believed to have been commended

definitions.meaning: given praise or recognition for something done

explanation.definitionFit: To credit a story is to accept it as true; to be credited with a deed is to be praised for it.

clue.text: Train following

definitions.meaning: a group of attendants who follow an important person
a body of followers or supporters

explanation.definitionFit: A royal retinue is the train of attendants, the following, that accompanies a monarch.

clue.text: Stupid as I have one over the eight

parts.note: one more than eight is nine; in British slang the phrase also means slightly drunk

explanation.surface: A drinker admits they are being silly, having had one too many.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one over the eight' is British slang for tipsy, but here it is plain arithmetic.
explanation.definitionFit: Asinine means donkey-like, hence silly or foolish.

clue.text: Trade vehicle I took to the cape

parts.note: a bus is a road vehicle
ness is a word for a headland or cape, as in Scottish place names

explanation.surface: A traveller describes taking a coach out to a headland.
explanation.definitionFit: Business and trade both mean commerce, the buying and selling of goods.

clue.text: Hits on revolutionary religion

indicators.note: revolutionary suggests the letters are overturned and rearranged

explanation.surface: Seems to describe a radical faith that strikes repeatedly.
explanation.definitionFit: Shinto is the indigenous religion of Japan, centred on worship of spirits called kami.

clue.text: A heavy meal?

parts.note: reads as a big dinner, but points to food that sits heavily in the stomach

explanation.walkthrough: Stodge is British slang for heavy, filling food such as suet puddings.
explanation.definitionFit: Stodge is starchy, filling food that leaves one feeling weighed down.

clue.text: Cheerless head of department back

indicators.note: head of picks the first letter of the following word

parts.note: the rear is the back

explanation.definitionFit: Drear is a poetic form of dreary, meaning dull and gloomy.

clue.text: Singular lashings of cream!

parts.note: lashings looks like plenty of cream, but a set of lashes is a beating, and cream for beating has its own name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lashings' means plenty in British English, but a single bout of lashing is a beating, and beating cream is the other sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A whipping is a beating with lashes, and whipping cream is cream thick enough to beat stiff.

clue.text: Whole triangle was redrawn

indicators.note: redrawn says the letters of the shape's name are laid out afresh

explanation.surface: A complete triangle was sketched again.
explanation.definitionFit: Integral means complete, forming an undivided unit.

clue.text: Some petty ranting from an oppressive leader

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.definitionFit: A cruel absolute ruler is the classic despot who oppresses his people.

clue.text: Help could be finer in Rose's home

indicators.note: in places the shuffled letters inside the rose's home

parts.note: a rose grows in a bed, so a bed is its home

indicators.note: could be suggests the letters might take another form

explanation.surface: Seems to say a helper might improve on Rose's house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like a woman's name, but it is the flower, and a flower bed is where it lives; 'could be' signals the shuffle and 'in' the container.
explanation.definitionFit: To befriend someone is to offer support and kindness, a form of helping.
